lessons.title: Complete Google Workspace Tutorial
objectives: Know what each Workspace app is for and which to open for a given job
Understand that everything saves to Drive, and what that changes
Set yourself up so the rest of this course works on your machine and your bundle
lessons.notes:
WHAT WORKSPACE IS: a set of apps that live in your browser and save to the same place. Docs for writing, Sheets for numbers, Slides for presentations, Drive to hold all of it, Gmail for mail, Calendar for time, Meet for calls, Forms for collecting answers from people.

THE ONE IDEA THAT MAKES EVERYTHING ELSE MAKE SENSE: THERE IS NO SAVE BUTTON. Every change is written as you type. There is no work lost because the power went, and there is no such thing as the latest version sitting on somebody's flash disk. That single difference is why offices move to it, and it takes a while to trust.

WHAT A FREE ACCOUNT GIVES YOU. An ordinary Gmail account gets every one of these apps at no cost, with 15GB shared across Drive, Gmail and Photos. That is years of documents and spreadsheets, and not very much video. Paid Workspace adds an address at your own domain, more storage and admin controls. You do not need it for this course or for paid work.

WHICH APP FOR WHICH JOB, because beginners lose hours here. Anything with rows and calculations belongs in Sheets, never in a table inside Docs. Anything a person will read as a document belongs in Docs. Anything you need to collect from many people belongs in Forms, which writes its answers straight into a Sheet for you.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the three things that actually decide whether this works for you where you are.

OFFLINE ACCESS. These apps assume a connection and yours will drop. Turn on offline access for Drive in Chrome BEFORE you need it. It is one setting, and it lets you keep working on recently opened files with no connection at all, syncing when you come back. Set it today, not on the afternoon the connection fails.

DATA COST. Loading a document is cheap. A video call is not - a Meet call uses far more bundle in an hour than a whole day of editing documents. Join audio-only and turn your camera off when the bundle is thin, and say so; nobody minds.

THE PHONE IS A REAL OPTION, not a poor substitute. The mobile apps are good enough to read, comment, reply and make small edits. Serious spreadsheet work wants a keyboard, but a great deal of the assistant work this course leads to is triage, and a phone does that perfectly well.
lessons.practice: Open Drive and create one folder for this course. Inside it create a Doc, a Sheet and a Slides file, name each one properly, and close them without saving anything. Reopen Drive and confirm all three are there with your text in them. Then turn on offline access in Chrome and confirm a file still opens with your connection switched off.

quiz.question: What replaces the save button in Google Workspace?
options: Nothing - every change is written as you type
A save button hidden in the File menu
An automatic save every ten minutes
Downloading the file when you finish

quiz.question: When should offline access be switched on?
options: Today, before you need it - not on the day the connection fails
Only when travelling
It is on by default and needs no action
Only on a paid Workspace account

lessons.title: Work Smarter with Google's Productivity Tools
objectives: Find any file in seconds instead of browsing folders
Build the small habits that make the tools genuinely fast
Stop the version-by-email habit that wastes whole offices' time
lessons.notes:
SEARCH BEATS FILING. Drive search looks INSIDE your documents, not just at their names. Three search habits save more time than any folder scheme ever will: search by who owns it, search by what kind of file it is, and search for a phrase you remember from inside it.

NAME FILES SO A STRANGER COULD FIND THEM. Date first in year-month-day order, then what it is, then who it is for: 2026-09-24 Invoice Mwangi Hardware. Sorted alphabetically, that list is also sorted by date, for free. Untitled document is the commonest single waste in any office.

STOP EMAILING ATTACHMENTS. The version-by-email habit - final, final2, final_really_last - is the exact thing Workspace exists to end. SEND A LINK. One file, one truth, everybody looking at the current version. The moment you attach a copy you have created a second version that will disagree with the first, and somebody will act on the wrong one.

TEMPLATES. Anything you write more than twice - an invoice, a quotation, a weekly report - becomes a template. Make a copy of it each time and never edit the original.

THE SHORTCUTS WORTH TEN MINUTES: the one that opens search, the one that pastes WITHOUT formatting, which cleans up the mess you get copying from a website, and the one that inserts a link.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - three things that matter more than any shortcut.

KEEP CLIENT WORK OUT OF YOUR PERSONAL ACCOUNT. If you are going to do paid work, use a separate account for it. When a client relationship ends you want to hand everything over cleanly, and your family photos should never be one misclick away from a shared folder.

SWITCH ON TWO-FACTOR AUTHENTICATION TODAY. Your Google account is now your filing cabinet, your mail, your client work and your recovery route for every other account you own. Somebody with your password has all of it. This is fifteen minutes and it is the highest-value quarter hour in this course.

YOU ARE HANDLING SOMEBODY ELSE'S PERSONAL DATA the moment you touch a client's customer list, staff records or contact sheet. Under Kenya's Data Protection Act the practical duties are simple and worth doing from the first job: hold only what you actually need, never copy it into your personal drive, and delete it when the work ends.
lessons.practice: Rename five badly named files using date-first naming. Then find one file using search alone, without opening a single folder. Make a template of something you write repeatedly and save it with COPY ME in the name. Finally, switch on two-factor authentication on the account you will use for work.

quiz.question: Why send a link rather than an attachment?
options: An attachment creates a second version that will disagree with the first
Attachments are always too large to send
Links load faster on a phone
Gmail blocks most attachments

quiz.question: What should you do before taking on client work in Workspace?
options: Use a separate account for it and switch on two-factor authentication
Upgrade to a paid Workspace plan
Buy a custom domain name
Install the desktop versions of the apps

lessons.title: Gmail Tutorial for Beginners - 2026 Update
objectives: Get an inbox to empty and keep it there
Use labels, filters and search instead of reading everything twice
Write mail that actually gets a reply, and spot the mail that is trying to rob you
lessons.notes:
THE INBOX IS A TO-DO LIST, NOT A FILING CABINET. Every message is one of three things: something you must do, something you want to keep, or rubbish. ARCHIVE keeps a message and takes it out of the inbox - it is not delete, and search still finds it instantly. Learn archive and half the problem disappears.

LABELS, NOT FOLDERS. One message can carry several labels at once, which is why they beat folders. Do not build twenty of them. Three or four that match how you actually work is plenty, and more than that becomes its own chore.

FILTERS DO THE SORTING BEFORE YOU EVER SEE IT. Everything from this sender gets that label and skips the inbox. Ten minutes setting up filters buys back an hour a week, every week.

SEARCH PROPERLY: from a particular sender, with an attachment, before a date. Searching beats scrolling every single time, and the search box accepts all three at once.

WRITING MAIL THAT WORKS. A subject line that says the actual thing, not Hello. The ask in the first sentence, because people read one sentence and decide. Short paragraphs. ONE REQUEST PER MESSAGE. If you need it by a date, write the date.

SNOOZE brings a message back when you can actually act on it. SCHEDULE SEND lets you write at eleven at night and deliver at eight in the morning, which matters when your client is in another time zone and you would rather not look like you never sleep.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the part that costs people real money here.

RECOGNISING A FRAUDULENT MAIL. The pattern is always the same three things: urgency, an unexpected link, and a request for a password, a code or a payment. No real bank, employer or service asks for your password or an M-Pesa PIN by email, ever. Hover over a link and read the address it actually goes to before you click; the name in the sender field is decoration and can say anything at all.

THE ONE THAT CATCHES BUSINESSES: a supplier you know suddenly mails you NEW BANK DETAILS, politely, with an invoice attached. Phone them on the number you already had - never the number in that message - and confirm before paying a shilling. This exact fraud has taken real money from real Kenyan businesses, and it works precisely because the mail looks completely ordinary.

A SIGNATURE with your name, what you do and a phone number takes two minutes and is the first thing a client judges.
lessons.practice: Take your inbox to empty by archiving or acting on everything in it. Create one filter that labels mail from a frequent sender and skips the inbox. Write a proper signature. Then open your spam folder, pick one message, and write down the three warning signs in it.

quiz.question: What does Archive do to a message?
options: Keeps it and removes it from the inbox - search still finds it
Deletes it after thirty days
Moves it to spam
Marks it as unread for later

quiz.question: A supplier emails you new bank details for an invoice. What should you do?
options: Phone them on the number you already had - never the one in the message - before paying
Reply to the message asking them to confirm
Pay it, since the invoice matches what you expected
Forward it to your bank for checking

lessons.title: Google Sheets Tutorial for Beginners
objectives: Build a sheet that stays usable as it grows
Use the handful of functions that do most real work
Avoid the layout mistakes that make a sheet impossible to analyse later
lessons.notes:
ONE ROW PER THING, ONE COLUMN PER FACT. That is the whole discipline and everything else follows from it. A row is one sale, one student, one expense. A column is one fact about that thing - the date, the item, the amount, who it was for. Almost every hour anyone ever spends fighting a spreadsheet traces back to breaking this one rule.

NO BLANK ROWS INSIDE YOUR DATA. No merged cells. Headers in row 1 and nowhere else. MERGED CELLS LOOK TIDY AND BREAK EVERYTHING - sorting, filtering, and every function you will later want to use. Widen the column instead.

THE FUNCTIONS THAT DO MOST OF THE WORK: SUM, AVERAGE and COUNT, then the two that really earn their keep - SUMIF and COUNTIF, which total or count only the rows matching a condition. Most real reporting anybody pays for is SUMIF underneath.

ABSOLUTE REFERENCES. When you copy a formula down a column, its references move with it. A reference written with dollar signs does not move. This is the single commonest cause of a formula that is right in the first row and quietly wrong in every row after it - and quietly wrong is far worse than broken, because nobody notices.

FREEZE THE HEADER ROW and turn on filters. Two clicks each, and they are the difference between a long sheet you can work with and one you dread opening.

FORMAT DATES AS DATES and numbers as numbers. A date stored as text will not sort and will not subtract. Set the spreadsheet locale so dates read in the order you actually write them.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - what a tutorial will not tell you about doing this for money.

KEEP RAW DATA AND REPORTS ON SEPARATE TABS. Paste exactly what you received onto one tab and never touch it. Build every summary on another tab that refers to it. When the client sends a corrected file - and they will - you replace one tab instead of rebuilding a day's work.

SHILLINGS. Use the currency format rather than typing KSh into the cell, because text does not add up and you will not notice until the total is wrong.

MAKE IT SURVIVE SOMEBODY ELSE. A short note at the top saying what this sheet is, where its data comes from and who maintains it turns a personal file into something a business can actually rely on. That difference is precisely what clients are paying for.
lessons.practice: Build a sheet of twenty real transactions - one row each, with date, category and amount columns. Freeze the header row, turn on filters, and format the amounts as currency. Then total by category using SUMIF and copy the formula down, using absolute references so every row stays correct. Check the last row by hand.

quiz.question: What is the core layout rule for a usable sheet?
options: One row per thing, one column per fact about it
One tab per month
Headers repeated every twenty rows
Totals at the top of each column

quiz.question: Why are merged cells a problem?
options: They break sorting, filtering and the functions you will want later
They make the file larger
They cannot be printed
They are not supported on mobile

lessons.title: Google Sheets QUERY Function for Pivot-Style Reports
objectives: Pull a filtered, sorted, summarised table out of raw data with one formula
Read QUERY well enough to change it confidently rather than copying it
Know when QUERY is the right tool and when a pivot table is
lessons.notes:
WHAT QUERY DOES: it lets you ask a question of a range and get a table back - these columns, only these rows, sorted this way, grouped and totalled. One formula replaces a filter, a sort and a column of SUMIFs, and it rebuilds itself whenever the underlying data changes.

THE SHAPE is the range, then the question written in quotes. The clauses go in a fixed order: SELECT which columns you want, WHERE which rows qualify, GROUP BY what to total over, ORDER BY how to sort, LABEL to rename the headings.

COLUMNS ARE LETTERS, NOT HEADINGS. Inside the quoted question you refer to A, B, C - or Col1, Col2 when the range came from somewhere else. Beginners try to use the header text and get an error that does not explain itself.

GROUP BY IS THE POWERFUL PART. Select the category column and the sum of the amount column, group by the category, and you have produced in one formula what used to be a pivot table - and unlike a pivot table it is written down, readable and copyable.

WHERE WITH TEXT needs quotes inside quotes, which is the commonest error by a distance. BUILD IT IN PIECES: get SELECT working on its own, then add WHERE, then add GROUP BY. Never type the whole thing at once and hope.

QUERY OR A PIVOT TABLE? A pivot table is quicker to click together and better while you are still exploring what the data says. QUERY is better once you know, because the report must rebuild itself the same way every week and a formula does that without anyone remembering how.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO. THIS IS THE FUNCTION THAT TURNS YOU FROM SOMEBODY WHO KEEPS A SPREADSHEET INTO SOMEBODY WHO PRODUCES A REPORT, and reports are what people pay for. A client sending you a raw sales export every month does not want a tidier export back; they want the three numbers they make decisions on. Build the raw tab and the QUERY-driven summary tab once, and every month afterwards is a paste and a glance.

ONE CAUTION: QUERY IS FRAGILE ABOUT MIXED TYPES. A column holding numbers with the occasional text entry will make QUERY quietly drop rows rather than complain. If a total ever looks smaller than you expected, check that column before you check your formula.
lessons.practice: On a sheet of at least thirty rows, write a QUERY that returns only the rows in one category. Extend it to sort by amount, largest first. Then write a second QUERY that groups by category and totals the amounts. Finally type a word into one cell of the amount column and see what happens to your total.

quiz.question: What does GROUP BY let you do in a QUERY?
options: Total the rows for each category, producing a report without a pivot table
Sort the results alphabetically
Hide columns you do not need
Combine two separate sheets

quiz.question: A QUERY total looks smaller than expected. What should you check first?
options: Whether the numeric column contains stray text, which makes QUERY silently drop rows
Whether the sheet needs refreshing
Whether the range is frozen
Whether the file is shared

lessons.title: Google Apps Script for Beginners: Automating Sheets, Docs & Gmail
objectives: Understand what Apps Script is and what it can reach in your account
Write and run a first small script safely
Judge which office chores are actually worth scripting
lessons.notes:
WHAT IT IS: JavaScript that runs inside your own Google account and can read and write your Sheets, Docs, Gmail and Calendar. It is the automation layer almost nobody finds, and it is already free with the account you have.

WHERE IT LIVES: Extensions, then Apps Script, from inside a Sheet. The script belongs to that file and travels with it.

MAKE THE FIRST SCRIPT TRIVIAL - read one cell, write another cell - so that when a real one misbehaves later you already know what working looks like.

AUTHORISATION. The first run asks your permission and shows an unreviewed-app warning, because you are the unreviewed developer. READ WHAT IT IS ASKING FOR. The habit matters far more than this one case: a script that wants access to all your mail should make you stop and ask why it needs that.

TRIGGERS make a script run without you - on a schedule, or whenever the sheet is edited. A daily trigger that mails a one-line summary at seven in the morning is the classic first genuinely useful automation.

WHAT IT IS ACTUALLY GOOD FOR: moving data between sheets, generating a document from each row, sending one formatted message per row, tidying an import that arrives in the same messy shape every week. It is not for heavy computation.

ADDITION BEYOND THE VIDEO - the safety rules, because unlike a practice exercise this script holds your real mail and real files.

TEST ON A COPY. Duplicate the sheet and run it there first. A loop with one mistake in it overwrites four hundred rows in about a second, and there is no undo.

NEVER SEND MAIL IN A LOOP ON THE FIRST RUN. Write the message to the log instead of sending it, read the log, and only then switch sending on. People discover this rule by mailing a client list twice, and it is a bad way to learn it.

MIND THE QUOTAS. A free account has a daily limit on how much mail a script may send, and scripted bulk mail gets accounts flagged. Use it for the twenty messages you would otherwise have typed by hand, not for a marketing blast.

AND NEVER PUT A PASSWORD OR AN API KEY IN THE SCRIPT, for exactly the reason keys never belong in code anywhere - scripts get copied, shared and pasted into chats.
lessons.practice: Duplicate a sheet, then write a script on the copy that reads a column and writes a summary into a cell. Run it and read what the authorisation screen asks for before accepting. Then add a version that builds a message for each row and writes it to the log INSTEAD of sending it, and read the log without sending anything.

quiz.question: What should you do before running a script that writes many rows of real data?
options: Run it on a duplicate copy first, because a mistake overwrites everything with no undo
Add comments explaining each line
Ask Google to review the script
Run it outside working hours

quiz.question: How should a script that sends mail be tested?
options: Write each message to the log and read it, before enabling any sending
Send the first ten and check them
Send everything to yourself first
Run it twice and compare
